To fix (4)

To fix Power Analysis Check

What we found

We detected 2 potential power analyses.

Show details

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8’ to check the contents of 3 paragraphs that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

Some essential information could not be detected: effect_size_metric

power_id power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
1 apriori regression 114 0.05 0.8 0.10 other G*Power
2 apriori other 146 0.05 0.8 0.26 NA G*Power
power_id text
1 131 participants were recruited via the departmental participant pool, the staff community board and private communication at Swansea University. Exclusion criteria were an age under 18 years and a BMI under 18 kg/m 2, as well as food allergies or intolerances, a history of or a current diagnosed eating disorder, medications or medical conditions influencing appetite and/or taste perception, low English proficiency, being currently pregnant or breast feeding, guessing the true aim of the study, and having taken part in a previous study by the researchers. Based on these exclusion criteria, data from seven participants had to be excluded (1 was vegetarian, 3 guessed the aim, and 3 had a BMI (Body Mass Index) < 18kg/m 2 ), which left data from 124 participants for analyses. This exceeded the 114 participants needed based on an a-priori sample size calculations in G*Power (Faul et al., 2009): multiple linear regression model with α-error probability of 0.05, statistical power of 0.8, three predictors (manipulation as predictor, restraint as moderator, and the interaction) and a small to medium effect size of f² = 0.1 (based on Price et al., 2016).
2 In total, 3 participants had to be excluded (1 guessed the exact aim and 2 had a BMI < 18 kg/mfoot_2 ) leaving data of 187 participants for analyses. According to the a-priori sample size calculation based on an ANCOVA in G*Power (Faul et al., 2009), 146 participants would have been needed to get a power of 0.8 with an effect size of 0.26 (based on study 1), numerator df=2, α-error=0.05, covariates=9, and number of groups=3.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 1 imprecise p value out of 45 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p<.05 Figure 2 -Interaction between condition and rigid restraint on intake of sweet products. * indicates a significant difference between conditions at a certain level of cognitive restraint, and Ɨ a significant relationship between intake and restraint for a specific condition, both at a level of p<.05.

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To fix Codebook Check

What we found

We found no codebook or README documentation for the 232 extracted data columns.

Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 4 codebook/README/label sources and 232 data columns across 4 files.

No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.

To check (3)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 24 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence

README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including ‘README’ in the name of your overview document.

Study/Repository Mismatch

The studies named in the manuscript do not match how the repository’s files are grouped: the repository separates out a study (ex3) not named in the manuscript. Check that every study has its own clearly-named folder or file prefix, and that the folder names match how the manuscript refers to each study.

File Naming

File names should be machine-parseable: no spaces or special characters, and every file should be classifiable by name or extension. We found 33 naming problems that should be fixed, and 4 files with a naming suggestion (not required, but a good habit).

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

Methods: Across two pre-registered experimental studies, participants were randomly allocated to either food-related EFT or control (activity-based EFT).

Across two studies, participants were told that they would receive either a high-, low-or very-low-calorie dinner later during the day -the food EFT (vs control not related to food).

131 participants were recruited via the departmental participant pool, the staff community board and private communication at Swansea University.

Based on these exclusion criteria, data from seven participants had to be excluded (1 was vegetarian, 3 guessed the aim, and 3 had a BMI (Body Mass Index) < 18kg/m 2 ), which left data from 124 participants for analyses.

The study was approved by the School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee at Swansea University, informed consent was obtained, and pre-registered at the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://osf.io/pydvz/; DOI: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/PYDVZ).

The study followed a between subject design and participants were randomly allocated to the experimental or control condition (block randomisation of 10 participants per block using http://www.random.org/).

Participants were presented with a range of snacks and were instructed to rate the sweetness, saltiness, bitterness, sourness, crunchiness, softness, liking, and healthiness of each food on a 100mm Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) to distract from the real aim of assessing intake (sensory data not otherwise used in the analysis).

Participants were invited to the study between 14.00 and 18.30 to increase consistency and the likelihood that they had eaten lunch but not dinner (similar to e.g., Higgs et al., 2008).

As can be seen in Table 1, comparable numbers of participants were in the control and experimental condition (49.2% vs 50.8%, respectively), with a similar distribution of female and male participants.

However, this hypothesised difference in snack intake would only be evident when participants were lower in (flexible, rigid and cognitive) restraint (similar to findings of study 1).

Methods 190 participants were recruited in the same way as in study 1, which included a buffer for possible exclusion of data.

In total, 3 participants had to be excluded (1 guessed the exact aim and 2 had a BMI < 18 kg/mfoot_2 ) leaving data of 187 participants for analyses.

Participants were equally distributed between the three conditions and had similar characteristics (see Table 4).

Firstly, since participants were thinking about their own eating plans for the rest of the day of testing, these plans could not be influenced and standardised.

However, there is the possibility that participants compensated for the snack consumption by having a smaller dinner.

Ethics approval statement:

The study was approved by the School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee at Swansea University, informed consent was obtained, and pre-registered at the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://osf.io/pydvz/; DOI: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/PYDVZ).

The study was pre-registered at OSF (https://osf.io/2pqbr/?view_only=a2d70b4b4b6c4e1e9618c39401c37c0c DOI: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/2PQBR), approved by the Ethics Committee of the Department for Psychology of Swansea University, and informed consent obtained.

research_questions We want to investigate the association between priming of prospective memory for eating plans and opportunistic snack intake and the possible effects of personality traits and trait tendencies to plan indulgences.

1. Confirmatory analysis:
In a moderation analysis we want to investigate the association between priming of participants to think about eating plans for the rest of the day and intake, and if trait tendencies to plan indulgences moderates this interaction. We will take following possible covariates into account: eating traits (DEBQ, flexible and rigid restraint sub-scales, craving, impulsiveness), time perspective, age, gender, BMI, hunger, liking, desire to eat, perceived healthiness and mood (PANAS). First, we will correlate them with intake and only use variable as covariates which are significantly correlated with intake,

2. Exploratory analysis:
a. In an exploratory moderation analysis, we are also interested if time perspective, impulsiveness and restrained eating moderate the association between the priming and intake, as well as the moderation by trait tendencies to plan indulgences while taking a series of covariates into account. We will take the same covariates as in the confirmatory analysis into account and follow the same procedure.
b. Additionally, we want to investigate possible influences of personality and eating traits on the perceived effectiveness of planning indulgence to reduce intake of snacks.
c. During initial testing of the wording of the priming, participants did not mention snacks. Therefore we are interested if snacks might not be planned opposed to meals and if that has an influence on intake.
d. We are further interested if people with trait tendencies to plan indulgences mention snacks in the priming. To research question 1:
We hypothesis an association between priming and intake as well as a moderating role of the trait tendencies to plan indulgence. We also investigate the potential role of following covariates: eating traits (DEBQ, flexible and rigid restraint sub-scales, craving, impulsiveness), time perspective, age, gender, BMI, hunger, liking, desire to eat, perceived healthiness and mood (PANAS), if they correlate significantely with intake.
We predict that the intervention group which thinks about future eating plans will consume fewer snacks in the taste test compared to the control group which thinks about future plans in general. This effect will be stronger for participants who do not normally plan indulgences. 		We want to replicate and expand on the findings of our previous study (OSF registration: ‘Association between prospective memory of eating plans and snack intake, and influence of personality and trait tendencies to plan indulgence on this association’). This study showed that the influence of a prime for prospective memory of eating plans on opportunistic snack intake was moderated by flexible restraint, rigid restraint and cognitive restraint (measured by the Dutch Eating Behaviour Questionnaire (DEBQ)). To explore if these results are specific to thinking about foods on the same day versus the next day, we will now add an additional intervention group (‘Plan tomorrow’s food’). 1) A confirmatory moderation analysis aims to replicate previous findings. Therefore the moderating role of restraint (flexible restraint, rigid restraint and cognitive restraint (DEBQ)) on the association between priming (‘Plan today’s food’, ‘Plan tomorrow’s food’, ‘Plan today’s activities’ group) and snack intake will be assessed. 2) In an exploratory analysis time perspective, impulsiveness, emotional eating, external eating and disinhibition will be taken into account as additional moderators. To research question 1) We predict that restrained eating has a moderating role in the association between priming and intake. Participants with lower restraint (flexible, rigid and cognitive restraint) eat significantly less in the control condition compared to the intervention groups and most in the ‘Plan today’s food’ group. We want to replicate and expand on the findings of our previous study (OSF registration: ‘Association between prospective memory of eating plans and snack intake, and influence of personality and trait tendencies to plan indulgence on this association’). This study showed that the influence of a prime for prospective memory of eating plans on opportunistic snack intake was moderated by flexible restraint, rigid restraint and cognitive restraint (measured by the Dutch Eating Behaviour Questionnaire (DEBQ)). To explore if these results are specific to thinking about foods on the same day versus the next day, we will now add an additional intervention group (‘Plan tomorrow’s food’). 1) A confirmatory moderation analysis aims to replicate previous findings. Therefore the moderating role of restraint (flexible restraint, rigid restraint and cognitive restraint (DEBQ)) on the association between priming (‘Plan today’s food’, ‘Plan tomorrow’s food’, ‘Plan today’s activities’ group) and snack intake will be assessed. 2) In an exploratory analysis time perspective, impulsiveness, emotional eating, external eating and disinhibition will be taken into account as additional moderators. sample_size_rationale The power calculation to perform a moderation analysis is based on a multiple linear regression and conducted in G*Power 3.1.9.2 (Faul, Erdfelder, Buchner, and Lang, 2009; Faul, Erdfelder, Lang, and Buchner, 2007). Following parameters were used: effect size f2 = 0.1 (small to medium effect size based on Price, Higgs, and Lee (2016)), α-error=0.05, power=0.8, predictors=3. The estimated sample size needed is 114 participants. However, we aim for 130 participants to build in a buffer for discarded data due to cases such as missing data, outliers or participants who guessed the real purpose of the study. To calculate the sample size, we first calculated the effect size of the moderation analysis in the previous study in G*Power 3.1.9.2 (Faul, Erdfelder, Buchner, and Lang, 2009; Faul, Erdfelder, Lang, and Buchner, 2007). The analysis was based on an ANCOVA – sensitivity analysis with following parameter: α-error=0.05, power=0.8, total sample size=120, groups=2 and covariates=9. The estimated effect size was 0.26. This effect size was applied in the power calculation based on an ANCOVA – a priori analysis. Additionally an α-error=0.05, power=0.8, groups=3 and covariates=9 were used. The estimated sample size needed is 146 participants. Based on the sample size of 60 participants per group in the previous study, we aim for 190 to replicate previous findings and build in a buffer for discarded data due to cases such as missing data, outliers or participants who guessed the real purpose of the study. This number also covers the estimated 146 participants of the power calculation. manipulated_variables Participants will randomly be assigned to the intervention or control condition. In the ‘plan today’s food’ intervention condition participants have to write down what they will eat over the rest of the day. In the ‘plan tomorrow’s food’ intervention condition participants have to write down what they will eat the next day. In the control condition they have to indicate their general plans for the rest of the day. - Desire to eat: “How strong is your desire to eat?” : VAS scale ‘not at all’ – ‘extremely’ (before and after taste test)

indices BMI will be calculated by using following equation: weight/(height^2)

The Balanced Time Perspective (BTP) will be assessed using the Deviation from the Balanced Time Perspective (DBTP; Stolarski, Bitner, and Zimbardo, 2011; Zhang, Howell, and Stolarski, 2013). P. G. Zimbardo and Boyd (1999) define BTP as “an idealized mental framework that allows individuals to flexibly switch temporal frames among past, future, and present depending on situational demands, resource assessments, or personal and social appraisals.” The DBTP is calculated applying following equation: DBTP=√((oPN-ePN)2+(oPP-ePP)2+(oPF-ePF)2+(oPH-ePH)2+(oF-eF)^2 ) oPN standing for the optimal time perspective (in this case Past-Negative) and ePN for the empirical time perspective (in this case Past-Negative). For the optimal values we followed P. Zimbardo and Boyd (2014) proposal: a ‘high’ score on Past-Positive is defines as 3.67, a ‘moderately high’ score on Present-Hedonistic as 4.33 and Future as 3.69, and a ‘low’ score on Past-Negative and Present-Fatalistic as 2.10 and 1.67, respectively. A DBTP of close to zero stands for an almost perfectly balanced time perspective. On the other hand, the higher the DBTP value the more the individual’s time perspective deviates from the optimal BTP. 		Self-reported BMI will be calculated by using following equation: weight/(height^2). In contrast to the previous study (‘Association between prospective memory of eating plans and snack intake, and influence of personality and trait tendencies to plan indulgence on this association’) weight and height will not be measured by the researcher due to time restrictions. Additionally there was a significant correlation between measured and self-reported BMI in previous study (r(123)=.939, p smaller than .000), showing that self-reported BMI is a valid representation of the measured BMI. - The Balanced Time Perspective (BTP) will be assessed using the Deviation from the Balanced Time Perspective (DBTP; Stolarski, Bitner, and Zimbardo, 2011; Zhang, Howell, and Stolarski, 2013). Multiple regression analysis: To investigate possible influences of personality and eating traits on the perceived effectiveness of planning indulgence to reduce intake of snacks, a multiple regression analysis will be performed. The personality and eating traits will be the independent variables and effectiveness as dependent variable.
    c. Linear regression analysis: During testing of the wording of the priming, participants did not mention snacks. So we are interested if snacks might not be planned opposed to meals and if that has an influence on intake. We use a linear regression analysis with ‘mentioning of snacks’ as independent variable and snack intake as dependent variable.
    d. We are further interested if people with trait tendencies to plan indulgences (IV) mention snacks in the priming (DV).

Code Check

Below, we describe some best coding practices and give the results of automatic evaluation of these practices in the code files below. This check may miss things or produce false positives if your scripts are less typical.

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). None of the files found could be checked for comments.

Missing Files

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

Packages / Dependencies

No packages/libraries were detected as loaded in the code files. (This check reads R and Python imports; other languages are not scanned for packages.) Even when no imports are detected, it is good practice to record the exact package versions the analysis depended on — see “Reproducible Environment” below.

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.
