The results of the moderation of the difference in intake between the conditions by other psychological and eating behaviour traits (time perspective, impulsivity, external and emotional eating) can be found in supplementary information C.

2.3. Interim discussion

The influence of EFT on snack intake was assessed by letting participants think about food-based compared to activity-based plans prior to a bogus taste test. Additionally, the interaction of EFT with restrained eating was explored.

Results failed to support the hypothesis, as there was no difference between the conditions in (sweet, savoury and total) intake. In the exploratory analysis, restraint only moderated the difference in condition on sweet snack intake. Intake increased with higher restraint, but only in the control condition, similarly to Tomarken and Kirschenbaum (1984). It seems that the experimental manipulation mitigated against the increase in intake associated with restraint observed within the control condition. While the goal-conflict model suggests that people with higher restrained might increase attention towards food if placed in front of them due to the conflict between their goal of enjoyment in the moment and the goal of weight management (Polivy & Herman, 2017; Stroebe, 2022), the EFT manipulation seem to have reduced this conflict. This could have led to similar intakes between high and low restrained eaters. An explanation for the equivalent results might be that most participants described their dinner in the experimental condition which was not congruent with the snacks offered in the present study. Indeed, Fedoroff et al. (2003) suggests that attention towards and intake of food in restrained eaters might only increase if food offered and the future episode is congruent, which present findings might support.

There was a significantly higher intake of sweet products for participants in the experimental condition, when cognitive, flexible and rigid restraint were low. These findings are in line with previous literature which found significantly higher intake in the food EFT condition compared to the control condition in unrestrained eaters (Tomarken & Kirschenbaum, 1984). A possible explanation might be that high restrained eaters already use considerable cognitive resources for restricting their intake, therefore, based on the counteractive control theory (Smeets et al., 2013), this may leave little resource for further cognitive activity. The same pattern was observed with flexible and rigid restraint (Westenhoefer et al., 2013).

In accordance with the present results, previous research has demonstrated that restraint only influences intake of sweet products but not savoury ones (Tomarken & Kirschenbaum, 1984). A possible explanation could be that savoury snacks were regarded as more healthy than sweet snacks and therefore participants did not use restraint as much to reduce intake (related-sample Wilcoxon signed rank test: Z = -9.08, p < .001).

However, the results should be interpreted with caution, as effects that were initially significantly did not withstand correction for multiple comparisons and explained only a very modest amount of variance. Additionally, the influence of restraint on the effect of condition on sweet and savoury intake was exploratory and should be replicated.

Therefore, in Study 2, we aimed to replicate the results with a pre-determined focus on restrained eating -due to the significant moderating effect of restrained eating on intake in Study 1 and previous studies (e.g., Tomarken & Kirschenbaum, 1984). Many EFT studies let participants create cues about future events which are further in the future than in Study 1, e.g., 1 month (e.g., Dassen et al., 2016) as health goals or events are often further in the future. However, meal plans usually span a short period of time (e.g., the same or next day). Participants in Gatzemeier et al. (2019) talked about planning indulgences for the same evening or next weekend. This seems to indicate that they use the strategy of planning to manage temptations in the moment of temptation, not only by thinking about the same day, but also a few days ahead. We were therefore interested in whether thinking about the meals for the next day could also influence intake in the current moment (and whether this is moderated by dietary restraint).

3. Study 2

In Gatzemeier et al. (2019), some participants thought about their food intake later that day (similar to study 1), while others imagined the food consumed later in the week, i.e., the weekend. Leaning on the Episodic memory (EM) literature, a second manipulation condition was added to the present study: food-based plans for the next day.

Similar to thinking about an event in one's own future (EFT), EM describes remembering and "reexperiencing" a specific event in one's own past (Tulving, 1972). These concepts are cognitively very similar (Szpunar, 2010) and EM (writing down the last meal consumed) has been shown to lead to lower snack intake in the present moment (Higgs & Spetter, 2018; Robinson et al., 2013). However, this effect disappeared when participants thought about the meal they consumed the day before (Higgs et al., 2008).

Therefore, the aim of study 2 was to investigate the influence of greater time being passed between the event of the EFT manipulation (here food intake) and the immediate snack intake -similarly to the EM literature (Higgs, 2002; Higgs et al., 2008) and the finding by Gatzemeier et al. (2019) that people thought not only about their meal plan of the same day, but the weekend.

Based on study 1, the first objective of study 2 was to replicate the results of study 1 that restrained eating moderates the relationship between condition and intake. The second objective was to investigate if thinking about the meals for the next day influences snack intake.

It was predicted that the EFT condition 'same-day food EFT' would reduce intake compared to the EFT condition 'next-day food EFT' and the control condition (activity-based plans for the same day).

Additionally, it was hypothesised (pre-registered) that restrained eating would moderate the difference between conditions regarding snack intake. Participants would eat significantly less in the control condition (activity-based EFT) compared to the experimental groups (food-based EFTs), with most eaten in the 'same-day food EFT' group. However, this hypothesised difference in snack intake would only be evident when participants were lower in (flexible, rigid and cognitive) restraint (similar to findings of study 1).

3.1. Methods

>Methods 190 participants were recruited in the same way as in study 1, which included a buffer for possible exclusion of data.

3.1.1. Participants

In total, 3 participants had to be excluded (1 guessed the exact aim and 2 had a BMI < 18 kg/mfoot_2 ) leaving data of 187 participants for analyses. According to the a-priori sample size calculation based on an ANCOVA in G*Power (Faul et al., 2009), 146 participants would have been needed to get a power of 0.8 with an effect size of 0.26 (based on study 1), numerator df=2, α-error=0.05, covariates=9, and number of groups=3.

Exclusion criteria were the same as in study 1. The study was pre-registered at OSF (https://osf.io/2pqbr/?view_only=a2d70b4b4b6c4e1e9618c39401c37c0c DOI: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/2PQBR), approved by the Ethics Committee of the Department for Psychology of Swansea University, and informed consent obtained.

3.1.2. Materials and procedure

The design, materials, and procedures are the same as in study 1 with the following exceptions: 1) an additional experimental group was added.

Therefore, there was the control condition (activity-based plans for the rest of the day), experimental manipulation 1 (food-based plans for the rest of the day), and experimental manipulation 2 (food-based plans for the next day).

The exact text can be found in supplementary information A.

2) some products for the taste test were exchanged. Liking for the salted popcorn offered in study 1 (Tesco Stores Ltd., Cheshunt, UK) was low (M = 60.01 on a 100mm VAS scale) and instead 2.5g of Butterkist salted popcorn (Butterkist, Leicestershire, UK) was offered 2 . To be able to include vegetarians, the Haribo Star Mix was exchanged to the vegetarian Haribo Funny Mix (HARIBO Dunhills, Pontefract, UK). Also, information about eating style (vegetarian, vegan or omnivore) was assessed.

3) only self-reported measures of weight and height were used.

4) The cover story was slightly changed to the exploration whether daily routine have an influence on preferences for sweet and/ or salty tastes. The Cronbach's alphas can be found in Table 3.

3.1.3. Statistical analysis

For frequentist analyses IBM SPSS v25 was used with the PROCESS v3 macro for moderation analysis (Hayes, 2018). A significant threshold of p < .05 was implemented. JASP was utilised for Bayesian analysis (not mentioned in the pre-registration). Data were excluded if the data point was the upper/lower IQR +/-1.5 IQR identified with the help of boxplots (Kwak & Kim, 2017). Data and syntax can be found on OSF (https://osf.io/yq4n6%20 ).

The same analyses as in study 1 were conducted.

3.2. Results

>Results

3.2.1. Participants

Participants were equally distributed between the three conditions and had similar characteristics (see Table 4). They were mainly female (66.3%), young (M = 21.59 ± 5.75 years) and had a healthy BMI (M = 23.97 ± 5.11 kg/m 2 ). Like study 1, hunger, fullness, and desire to eat were similar across the conditions.

3.2.2. Covariates

Covariates for the analyses with overall, sweet and savoury snack intake are presented in Table 5, respectively. There were only significant differences between conditions for DBTP (χ 2 (2) = 6.42, p = 0.040) and ZTPI past negative TP (χ 2 (2) = 6.36, p = 0.042) which were also used as covariates. As in study 1, BMI was used as covariate due to its known relationship to food intake (Swinburn, Sacks, Lo, et al., 2009) and the difference in consumption after EFT between BMI categories (Segovia et al., 2020). PANAS: Positive and Negative Affect Schedule, ZTPI: Zimbardo Time Perspective Inventory, DBTP:

Deviation from the Balanced Time Perspective, FCQ-T: Food Craving Questionnaire -Trait, DEBQ: Dutch Eating Behaviour Questionnaire, BIS11: Barratt Impulsiveness Scale.

3.2.3. Confirmatory analysis

There were no significant differences between the conditions in overall intake in grams (control vs same-day food EFT: ΔF(1,144) = 0.59, ΔR2 = 0.00, p = .446; control vs next-day food EFT: ΔF(1,144) = 0.21, ΔR2 = 0.00, p = .651), with our Bayesian analysis suggesting substantial support for the null hypothesis (BF01 = 7.569).

When adding restraint as moderator to this relationship, no moderating effect by cognitive (F(2,140) = 2.59, ΔR2 = 0.03, p = .078, BF01 = 2.028), flexible (F(2,130) = 0.89, ΔR2 = 0.01, p = .415, BF01 = 2.141) or rigid restraint (F(2,130) = 2.02, ΔR2 = 0.02, p = .137, BF01 = 1.826) was found. Our Bayesian analyses suggested anecdotal support for the null hypothesis for flexible restraint but anecdotal evidence in favour of the alternative hypothesis for overall cognitive and rigid restraint.

3.2.4. Exploratory analysis

Similarly, there was no difference in sweet and savoury snack intake between conditions (sweet: control vs same-day food EFT: ΔF(1,151) = 3.32, ΔR2 = 0.01, p = .070; control vs next-day food EFT: ΔF(1,151) = 0.05, ΔR2 = 0.00, p = .823; savoury: control vs same-day food EFT: ΔF(1,138) = 0.61, ΔR2 = 0.00, p = .435; control vs next-day food EFT: ΔF(1,138) = 0.10, ΔR2 = 0.00, p = .748). Our Bayesian analyses suggested there was substantial to strong evidence in favour of the null hypothesis (sweet: BF01 = 6.593; savoury: BF01 =11.527).

There was no interaction between any form of restraint and condition on intake of sweet products (cognitive restraint: F(2,141) = 1.93, ΔR2 = 0.02, p = .150, BF01 = 2.021; flexible restraint: F(2,131) = 0.24, ΔR2 = 0.00, p = .788, BF01 = 2.183; rigid restraint: F(2,131) = 1.53, ΔR2 = 0.02, p = .221, BF01 = 1.963). However, for savoury snacks, flexible restraint tended to influence the association between condition and consumption, which was supported by anecdotal evidence for the alternative hypothesis by the bayes factor (flexible: F(2,129) = 3.03, ΔR2 = 0.03, p = .052, BF01 = 2.099; cognitive restraint: F(2,139) = 1.84, ΔR2 = 0.02, p = .193, BF01 = 1.544; rigid: F(2,129) = 1.76, ΔR2 = 0.02, p = .176, BF01 = 1.939). However, when adjusted for multiple comparisons, no significant moderation was found. As the interaction tended to significance, a simple slope analysis was run. Differences in savoury snack intake between the two manipulation conditions were found (Figure 3; ß = -0.91, s.e. = 0.38, t = -2.37, p = .019, 95% CI [-1.67, -0.15]), but not between the manipulations and the control condition (same-day food EFT vs control: ß = 0.72, s.e. = 0.40, t = 1.77, p = .078, 95% CI [-0.08, 1.51]; next-day food EFT vs control: ß = -0.20, s.e. = 0.39, t = -0.50, p = .615, 95% CI [-0.97, 0.58]).

Participants who thought about their eating plans for the next day tended to eat less of their savoury snack compared to participants who thought about their eating plans for that day, but only if they were very high in flexible restraint. As before, further traits were assessed as moderators. As the focus here is on restrained eating, the results of the moderation analyses with these other psychological and eating behaviour traits are in supplementary information D.

4. General discussion

Across two experimental studies, we aimed to investigate the influence of food-based Episodic Future Thinking (EFT) on snack intake and the possible effects of restraint on this association. However, the results did not show an effect of food-based EFT (neither same-day nor next-day EFT) on intake, contrary to our hypotheses and previous literature which looked at health-or event-based EFTs. Also, exploratory consideration of moderation by restrained eating yielded mixed effects.

There are a range of possible explanations why no effect of food-based EFT was observed. The effects of EFT might be very domain specific. A food-based EFT (independent of the time until the imagined event) might increase cue reactivity and attention towards food, and therefore increased wanting of food in the moment instead of focusing on the future (Boswell & Kober, 2016). On the other hand, a health goal EFT reinforces that snack intake might hinder the person's desired goals (O'Neill et al., 2016), which might lead to a decrease in intake. The increased cue reactivity and attention due to the food-based EFT, might have led to disinhibited eating, because the food-based EFT might not be strong enough to override the response to the initial thought of the food. Especially when consumption of snacks -when in front of the individual -might be established as habit. This can lead to automatic behaviours (e.g., eating) which are uncoupled from expected outcomes (e.g., long term weight gain) and therefore cannot be influenced by future thinking of foods (see also Guthrie et al., 2013). This might be more pronounced in individuals with low restraint since they tend not to restrict intake in order to lose weight. As some participants in the control condition (thinking about activities planned for the rest of the day) also thought about their eating plans, this might have also increased attention towards foods. Both conditions thinking about foods (even though to a different extend) might explain the non-significant difference in snack intake. This is in line with Downey et al. (2025), who proposed that there is no difference in effect of EFT depending on domain (e.g., food, health, family) on delay discounting. Only food was a moderator for the effect of EFT on delay discounting, but only when no covariates were included. However, only few studies included in this review experimentally manipulated the EFT domain as was done in the present study (Downey et al., 2025).

In the future, a standardised protocol for EFT studies should be developed as started by Hollis-Hansen et al. (2019) (after the beginning of both of the present studies). For this, different domains (foodbased, health-based and event-based EFTs) could be manipulated and compared to find the most promising avenue.

Additionally, EFT might be more effective when only one food is offered (as in, e.g., Vartanian et al., 2016). The present study offered a variety of snacks all at the same time -different tastes (from sweet to savoury) and textures (from soft to crunchy), as might be found at buffets or parties.

Therefore, the increased consumption associated with the presence of variety may have influenced our outcome (Raynor & Vadiveloo, 2018).

When looking at the second objective, the moderation on intake of sweet food by flexible, rigid and cognitive restraint could not be replicated in the second study, but flexible restraint interacted with condition on savoury snack intake, but only if the two manipulations (same-day and next-day foodbased plans) were compared. A reason for this difference might be that the sample size to examine the influence of condition on intake might have provided sufficient statistical power, but not for the moderation analyses, which requires a higher sample size due to the additional interaction between predictor and moderator. This is supported by our Bayesian analyses, which show anecdotal evidence in favour of the alternative hypotheses for most of the moderations. Additionally, a number of very small changes were implemented between study 1 and 2 such as exchange of the brand of popcorn and sweets to accommodate vegetarians. This could have impacted the comparability of the results. Therefore, the findings should be interpreted with caution. To decrease these limitations, more participants should be recruited to sufficiently power a moderation analysis and consistent snacks offered.

Methodological differences between previous and present studies might explain the differences in findings. This shows the impact of the formulation (e.g., health goal vs food-based EFT) and presentation of the EFT (once vs repeated during meal) on the efficacy of EFT. While research found a significant effect of EFT on intake (Ding et al., 2024), it might not be easily implemented in everyday life in a range of situations (e.g., not only at home, but also when having a meal out with friends).

When eating out of home with friends and family, which is associated with higher energy intake (Lachat et al., 2012), it might not be feasible to listen repeatedly to a cue. Therefore, future research should focus on identifying presentations which are easy to adopt in day-to-day life and subjectively effective. This can increase acceptance and implementation long-term (Bos et al., 2015). EFT could be an easy and cost-effective tool to manage intake with cues being created with the help of healthcare professionals, apps or websites.

A few limitations of the current study must be noted. Firstly, since participants were thinking about their own eating plans for the rest of the day of testing, these plans could not be influenced and standardised. Though more realistic, there might be many factors influencing the results which were not directly measured. The future foods may have differed in (1) calorie content, which was shown to influence intake (Tomarken & Kirschenbaum, 1984), (2) in flavour, possibly incongruent to the flavour of the snacks offered (Fedoroff et al., 2003), and (3) amount, since it was all the food until they went to bed without any further specification (meals vs. snack). Future studies should either offer or pretend to offer a standardised meal, similar to EM studies (Higgs, 2002; Higgs & Jones, 2013) and Tomarken and Kirschenbaum (1984). Secondly, some people ate all the snacks offered within the laboratory, which might have led to a ceiling effect. More food could be offered to identify greater differences between intakes. Thirdly, the presented studies only measured intake immediately after the experimental manipulation. However, there is the possibility that participants compensated for the snack consumption by having a smaller dinner. In previous research participants mentioned to schedule indulgences for the weekend (Gatzemeier et al., 2019), so they might have made a plan whilst within our laboratory to eat fewer tempting foods later to balance the snack intake during the study. This planned compensation could be examined by letting participants keep a food diary for a week (Johnson, 2002; Rutishauser, 2005). Fourthly, a range of analyses were conducted to investigate the influence of different psychological and eating behaviour traits on the effect of the EFT on snack intake. Additionally, the results from study 1 and 2 were inconsistent. Therefore, the results should be interpreted with caution as these were exploratory and might be underpowered. Future research should run the study again with a larger sample size and focussing on restrained eating to reduce the risk of type II and I errors, respectively. Fifthly, while covariates were determined via a two-step process and the use of a correlation matrix -a similar process as has been done previously (e.g., Price et al., 2017) -there is an increased risk of overfitting which is acknowledged. Therefore, future studies should consider using other methods to identify covariates as suggested by Sauer et al. (2013). Lastly, the participants in both studies were young (study 1: M=30 years and study 2: M=22 years) and mostly university students. Age is shown to influence snack intake (Si Hassen et al., 2018) as well as EFT (Schacter et al., 2018). Therefore, the results cannot be generalised and are likely only representing younger adults.

To conclude, no difference between food-based (same-day and next-day) and activity-based EFTs on snack intake was found. This might be because food-based EFTs do not necessarily align with health goals and are not excluding current intake. Therefore, health-based EFTs might be more effective.

When restraint was considered, results were mixed, possibly due to small sample sizes. Therefore, the study should be replicated with larger sample sizes.
